\section{Supplementary Methods}

\bmhead{S1. Label processing and units}
A site-year is one observation location (coordinates rounded to 0.0001$^\circ$) in one observation year; a cell-year is the mean over the sites that fall in one 1 km map cell in one year (Supplementary Table~S5). ABoVE version 2\cite{Moore2025} contains \nqcAboveRaw{} thaw-depth records; after restricting to probe measurements in August--October with an ALT between 0 and 300 cm within 45--80$^\circ$N, \nqcAboveKept{} records remained, and \nqcAboveEarly{} measurements from January--July were excluded as early-season values. CALM\cite{Streletskiy2025} contributed \nqcCalmSy{} site-years in Alaska and Canada, of which \nqcCalmNoloc{} could not be located, giving \nqcCalmCy{} site-years. ALLena\cite{Veremeeva2025} contains \nqcLenaRaw{} records, of which \nqcLenaEos{} are August--September values without the measurement-limit flag; the seasonal maximum per location and year gave \nqcLenaCy{} site-years. Of the \nqcTotalCy{} site-years of all years, \nqcTotalCyIn{} fall in 2010--2024 and have year-specific climate input. Multiple measurements at a site in a year were averaged, and the mean day of year was kept for the accumulation of thawing degree-days (TDD).

\bmhead{S2. Climate variables}
All climate variables are computed from monthly ERA5-Land means for the observation year of each site-year. TDD is the sum over the months of the year of the positive monthly mean air temperature multiplied by the number of days in the month; the cumulative TDD to the end of each month gives the value at the observation day by linear interpolation in the day of year. The freezing degree-days and the coldest monthly mean temperature are computed over the winter preceding the thaw season, from October of the previous year to April of the observation year. The snow water equivalent is averaged over the hydrological year ending in the observation year, from October of the previous year to September. The soil temperature is the annual mean of the top ERA5-Land soil layer (0--7 cm). Cells over sea in ERA5-Land use the nearest land cell within 0.2$^\circ$ and then within 0.5$^\circ$. The mean climate input used in Fig.~3a of the main text is the 2011--2024 mean of these yearly values (2010 is excluded because its winter variables are incomplete); all other analyses use the input of the observation year, and the yearly maps use the input of the mapped year with the TDD accumulated to 1 September.

\bmhead{S3. Products: extraction, coverage and training data}
The five products are published under open licences (Supplementary Table~S1). Wei et al.\cite{Wei2026}, Liu et al.\cite{Liu2024}, ESA CCI\cite{Westermann2024,Westermann2025} and Aalto et al.\cite{Aalto2018} cover the Northern Hemisphere permafrost region and are intended for use outside the regions of their training data; Yi and Kimball\cite{YiKimball2019} cover Alaska. Yearly products were sampled at the cell centre for the observation year: Wei et al. from the 1 km EPSG:3995 rasters, Liu et al. from the 1/120$^\circ$ rasters, ESA CCI v4 and v5 from the yearly NetCDF files, and Yi and Kimball from the Alaska NetCDF. Aalto et al. provide one value for 2000--2014. Wei et al. were trained on 201 CALM and GTN-P sites with 2,196 annual observations of 2000--2020 and publish the site coordinates; the median distance from our label cells to the nearest site is \ndistweiAkmed{} km in Alaska, \ndistweiLemed{} km in the Lena Delta and \ndistweiCamed{} km in Canada (Supplementary Fig.~S6). Liu et al. were trained on 2,966 site-years from CALM, an earlier version of the ABoVE data (2008--2020), ABCflux and Tibetan sites. ESA CCI is a process model driven by remotely sensed land-surface temperature and is not trained on ALT observations. Mean product biases by latitude band (prediction minus observation) were computed on the label site-years with a product value of the observation year.

\bmhead{S4. Product-anchored residual learning and SHAP}
In the product-anchored test, the product value $p$ of the observation year was recalibrated on the training fold as $a+bp$ (least squares), and the residual learner of the main model was trained on $y-(a+bp)$ with the same 23 features and $\lambda=0.5$. The test used the spatial-block folds of the main experiment and only the site-years with a product value. SHAP values\cite{Lundberg2017} were computed with CatBoost's exact tree algorithm for the residual model ($y-\hat{y}_P$) and the direct model, both fitted to all labels of a region, and summarised as the mean absolute value per feature and per feature group.

\bmhead{S5. Computing environment}
The CatBoost experiments (validation designs, covariate sets, label and transfer ladders, product-anchored test, SHAP) were run on 96-core cloud CPU nodes; the neural learners (MLP, TabM, FT-Transformer) on one NVIDIA A100 GPU; data preparation, map prediction and figures on a local server (CPU). Software: Python 3.9, CatBoost 1.2.10, PyTorch 2.6, scikit-learn 1.3, NumPy 1.26. All fits use fixed random seeds, and the three seeds of each experiment are averaged before scoring.

\section{Supplementary Figures}
\sifig{FigS1_stefan}{\textbf{Stefan relation within a season and among years.} (a) Samoylov 2015: cumulative TDD, probed thaw depth (daily mean $\pm$ 1 s.d.) and the Stefan curve. (b) Thaw depth against the square root of TDD accumulated to the measurement day at Samoylov (2015) and Kurungnakh (2020), with Stefan fits. (c) Deviation of ALT from the site mean against the deviation of $\sqrt{\mathrm{TDD}}$ at sites observed in four or more years (2010--2024); points outside the axis window are not drawn (46 of 2,161 site-years), the fits use all. (d) Stefan coefficient $E$ by region, source coefficient and recalibrated.}{fig:s1}
\sifig{FigS2_structures}{\textbf{Position of the physical information and choice of learner.} Difference in spatial-block RMSE from the recalibrated Stefan model for direct ML, physics-input ML, physics pseudo-labels and the physics-residual model (a), and for the physics-residual model and direct ML with five learners (b). Labels 2010--2024; bars are 95\% block-bootstrap intervals. The physics-residual model is the only structure whose gain is resolved in two regions with every learner, which is why it is the main model.}{fig:s2}
\sifig{FigS3_obs_pred_density}{\textbf{Observed against predicted ALT under spatial-block cross-validation.} All site-years of each region for the recalibrated Stefan model, the physics-residual model and direct ML (rows, regions; columns, methods); colour marks the density of site-years and the line is 1:1; RMSE and Pearson $r$ are printed. The recalibrated Stefan model predicts a narrow range of values because one coefficient cannot separate the sites of a region; the learned models spread the predictions along the 1:1 line. Direct ML has the lowest RMSE here because the test sites interleave with the training sites of the same region; its ranking reverses when a region is withheld (Fig.~3c).}{fig:s11}
\sifig{FigS4_shap}{\textbf{Contribution of the input groups to the residual and direct models.} Share of the mean absolute SHAP value of climate, terrain and soil variables (a) and the four largest inputs of the residual model in each region (b). Models fitted to all labels of 2010--2024. The residual learner draws mainly on soil and terrain, that is, on what the Stefan term does not contain.}{fig:s3}
\sifig{FigS5_label_ladder}{\textbf{Within-region label ladder.} Difference in RMSE from a Stefan model recalibrated on the same training labels, for the physics-residual model and direct ML, against the number of training labels drawn at random from the training folds of the spatial-block cross-validation (three draws per number, averaged; bands, 95\% block-bootstrap intervals). With 25--250 labels direct ML is worse than the recalibrated Stefan model in Alaska and Canada, whereas the physics-residual model improves on it from 25 labels in every region; direct ML overtakes it only when most of the region's labels are used. The transfer ladder is Fig.~4c of the main text.}{fig:s4}
\sifig{FigS6_training_sites}{\textbf{Distance to product training sites and differences between product maps and our map.} (a) Training sites of Wei et al. and the label cells of the three regions (2010--2024). (b) Cumulative share of label cells against the distance to the nearest training site of Wei et al.; the dashed line marks 25 km. (c) Mean difference between each product and our Alaska map of 2013 by latitude band, for cells at or below and above 600 m elevation (all 1 km cells with a value in both maps).}{fig:s6}
\sifig{FigS7_yearwise}{\textbf{RMSE per observation year.} Years with at least 30 site-years; rows, observation years; columns, the recalibrated Stefan model and the physics-residual model (spatial-block out-of-fold predictions with the climate input of that year) and the products of Wei et al. and Liu et al. (value of that year). Cell text, RMSE in cm; cell colour, difference from the RMSE of the physics-residual model in the same year (blue, lower; red, higher). Rows are the site-years with a value of Wei et al.; Liu et al. is scored on its subset (to 2020) and $n$ is the number of site-years of the row. The products are closest to our model in Alaska before 2018 and far from the observations in the Lena Delta in every year.}{fig:s5}
\sifig{FigS8_product_anchor}{\textbf{Product-anchored and Stefan-anchored residual learning.} RMSE on the label site-years with a value of Wei et al. for the observation year (Alaska and Canada 2010--2024, Lena Delta 2013--2021; $n$ is the number of site-years) under spatial-block cross-validation: the product as published, the product linearly recalibrated on the training folds (equation (10) of the main text), the recalibrated product with a residual learner, the recalibrated Stefan model and the physics-residual model. A residual learner also improves a product anchor, but the Stefan-anchored model remains the most accurate in every region.}{fig:s7}
\sifig{FigS9_site_series}{\textbf{Yearly series at the site with the most observed years in each region.} Observed ALT (open circles, joined) and spatial-block out-of-fold predictions for 2010--2024 (separate three-seed fit) at the site with the most observed years in (a) Alaska, (b) the Lena Delta and (c) Canada (NW): the physics-residual model at the observation day (squares) and with the TDD to 1 September (line, as the yearly maps), the recalibrated Stefan model with the TDD to 1 September, and the values of Wei et al. and Liu et al. where the product has a value at the cell (none at the Lena Delta site). The shaded years are the warmest and coldest thaw seasons of the region (regional mean TDD, Fig.~7d); the deepest observed values at the Alaska and Lena Delta sites fall in the warmest seasons (2019 and 2021), and the Canada site shows a level offset of about 20 cm that no model with the Stefan anchor removes.}{fig:s10}
\sifig{FigS10_map_detail}{\textbf{Detail of the 1 km maps and area of applicability.} (a--d) Mean ALT of 2011--2024 drawn as 1 km cells over hillshade in four windows: North Slope near Toolik (a) and Interior near Fairbanks (b) in Alaska (50 km), Samoylov and Kurungnakh in the Lena Delta (c, 24 km) and the Mackenzie Delta near Inuvik in Canada (d, 50 km); the colour scale is that of Fig.~7a--c. (e--g) Dissimilarity index of each cell divided by the threshold of the area of applicability (equation (11) of the main text; values above 1 lie outside the area and are drawn lighter in all maps) for Alaska, the Lena Delta and Canada (NW), with the windows of a--d; the index is the per-cell indicator of uncertainty, whereas the prediction interval is constant within a region.}{fig:s8}
\sifig{FigS11_correction_maps}{\textbf{Residual correction of the Stefan model.} Physics-residual minus recalibrated Stefan prediction per 1 km cell for the mean of the yearly maps of 2011--2024 in (a) Alaska, (b) the Lena Delta and (c) Canada (NW); negative values indicate that the residual learner lowers the Stefan estimate. The colour range is $\pm$10 cm (values beyond it are saturated); the 1 km values are interpolated to 250 m (Lena Delta) or 500 m (Alaska, Canada) for display.}{fig:s9}
